title: Objective tests of ecological models used to guide land management—A reply to Chambers et al. (2026)
content:
Our analysis revealed the utility of a climatic water-deficit metric as an indicator of R&R and moreover suggested a previously unknown scale mismatch in R&R indicators and landscape observations derived from plots. Chamber et al. (2026)'s scale argument agrees with our scale-mismatch conclusion. Their thoughtful response combines with our findings to improve understanding of the application context of climatic indicators of R&R—an important and impactful ecological concept and model.


Abstract

Good ecological models are objective, testable and lend themselves to improvement, especially when their parameters are derived and application contexts are not completely known. In Applestein & Germino (2025), we compared indicators of resistance to invasion and resilience to disturbance (R&R, a model) to post-fire vegetation patterns in burned sagebrush steppe threatened by wildfire-promoting exotic annuals such as cheatgrass. Chambers et al. (2026) argued our analysis was inappropriate and emphasized that it ‘characterize(ed) post-fire plant community composition at plot scales’. We measured but did not analyse or make main inferences of plant-community patterns at the plot scale. Species associations in plots were used to generate landscape-scale estimates of the amount each landscape was comprised of cheatgrass- or bunchgrass-dominated community associations. Our use matches how R&R indicators are used to plan management treatments. Moreover, plot-level data were used to parameterize R&R indicators, and thus are appropriate to parameterize landscape-scale evaluations of them. A priori published guidance on the appropriate scale of application, ideally quantitative sideboards, was and is still not available. We used the indices as predictors at the 30-m scale at which they were produced, in collaboration with the indices' developers. Variables that describe the 3D plot locations and sampling timing were required in the statistical analysis to address statistical inference against covariance. Their significance means other variables tested were less (or non-) explanatory, and we made no further inference regarding their generalizability or relevance to climate responses, contrary to the argument of Chambers et al. (2026). Synthesis and applications. Our analysis revealed the utility of a climatic water-deficit metric as an indicator of R&R and moreover suggested a previously unknown scale mismatch in R&R indicators and landscape observations derived from plots. Chamber et al. (2026)'s scale argument agrees with our scale-mismatch conclusion. Their thoughtful response combines with our findings to improve understanding of the application context of climatic indicators of R&R—an important and impactful ecological concept and model.
